actualDepthRangeMeters.note: FishBase lists 20-1000 m and notes the species is usually found from 20-200 m. OceanEye's 700 m display depth is a curated rare twilight encounter, supported as a product placement by deeper live ROV observations but not presented as the usual depth.

habitat: The giant oarfish has a worldwide distribution, having been found as far north as 72°N and as far south as 52°S, but is most commonly found in the tropics to middle latitudes, 180°W to 180°E.
summary: “It is the world's longest ray-finned fish. Its shape is ribbon-like, narrow laterally, with a dorsal fin along its entire length, stubby pectoral fins, and long, oar-shaped pelvic fins, from which its common name is derived.[3] Its coloration is silver and blue with spots of dark pigmentation, and its fins are crimson.” - Wiki

annotations.title: Source of "Sea Serpent"
annotations.body: "Its physical characteristics and undulating mode of swimming have led to speculation that it might be the source of many "sea serpent" sightings. In 2016, the TV show River Monsters concluded that the most likely origin of the sea serpent myth is the oarfish." - Wiki

annotations.title: Behavior
annotations.body:
"Little is known about oarfish behavior. It has been observed swimming by means of undulating its dorsal fin, and also swimming in a vertical position using undulatory movements of both its body and dorsal fin. In 2010, scientists filmed a giant oarfish in the Gulf of Mexico swimming in the mesopelagic layer, the first footage of a reliably identified R. glesne in its natural setting. The footage was caught during a survey, using an ROV in the vicinity of Thunder Horse PDQ, and shows the fish swimming in a columnar orientation, tail downward.

A 2016 episode of TV show River Monsters filmed two oarfish, most likely R. glesne, swimming in deep water in the middle of the Mediterranean Sea, off the coast of France. In season 8 episode 1, titled "Deep Sea Demon" (the 47th episode of the series), River Monsters host Jeremy Wade and his crew went to a specific buoy, anchored to the seabed by a single vertical chain, where previous sightings of an oarfish had been reported. At the buoy, the water is approximately 2.4 km (1.5 mi) deep. The rarely-sighted oarfish was reported to occasionally swim up and down the chain, sometimes as close as 9.1 m (30 ft) from the surface. During Wade's second diving attempt, done around nightfall, he successfully saw first one, then two living and healthy oarfish. Wade estimated the first oarfish was roughly 2.5 times Wade's height; unofficial reports list Wade's height as 1.83 m (6.0 ft) tall, meaning the oarfish was roughly 4.57 m (15.0 ft) long. The first oarfish seemed mildly curious but unafraid of Wade; it came close enough that Wade was able to reach out and gently touch it, to which the oarfish barely reacted. A little after this, the second oarfish swam up to Wade, leaving him diving in the water with two extremely rare fish. It is unknown exactly why the oarfish were there, whether they came to that location to feed, or whether or not they were a breeding pair. Both oarfish appeared to be using the buoy's chain as a point of reference in the sea. The oarfish were filmed swimming both vertically and horizontally (in reference to the vertical chain) while undulating their dorsal fins. Wade commented on how graceful and fast both oarfish were in the water. When resting next to the chain, both oarfish seemed to prefer being vertical, with their tails downward. After a while, both oarfish swam away unharmed." - Wiki

annotations.title: Self-amputation
annotations.body: "R. glesne shows evidence of self-amputation of the body posterior to the vent. This amputation can either be just involving the caudal fin and a small number of vertebrae, or it may be the entire posterior part of the body. As the organs of R. glesne are concentrated in the front portion of the body, these amputations do not damage any vital organs. These amputations are noted to occur several times throughout the lifetime of the fish (serial autotomy), and all fish over 1.5 m (4.9 ft) long have bodies shortened by this. It is unclear why these amputations occur, as oarfish have no documented natural predators, so it is unlikely to be a predation response. Despite a common misconception that oarfish are preyed on by sharks, no shark attacks on oarfish have been documented. There is one recorded instance of a pod of pilot whales attacking an oarfish, but they did not eat it." - Wiki

annotations.title: Conservation
annotations.body:
"R. glesne is not fished commercially, but it is an occasional bycatch in commercial nets. When cooked, the taste of an oarfish is described as "like paper." R. glesne was offered to a dog who regularly consumes fish, and was refused. Six people agreed to try fried oarfish and said that the taste was suitable, but the flesh was extremely flaccid, and overall objectionable.

The Egyptian deity Ḥȝyšš, of which 16 depictions are known, is described as a horse-headed snake god and found on coffins and sarcophagi. It has been proposed that this is a depiction of R. glesne, based on the similarity of the elongated fins and coloration.

The giant oarfish, and the related R. russelii, are sometimes known as "earthquake fish" because they are popularly believed to surface before and after an earthquake, although such correlation is not supported.

Due to their size, elongated bodies, and undulating swimming pattern, giant oarfish are presumed to be responsible for some sea serpent sightings. A 2016 episode of the TV series River Monsters, seeking to uncover the origin of the sea serpent myth, concluded that the most likely culprit was the oarfish. Formerly considered rare, the species is now suspected to be relatively common, although sightings of healthy specimens in their natural habitat are unusual." - Wiki

zh.actualDepthRangeNote: FishBase 记录为 20-1000 米，并注明通常见于 20-200 米。OceanEye 的 700 米是策展式罕见暮光相遇点；更深活体 ROV 观察支持这种产品放置，但不表示这是通常深度。
zh.habitat: 热带到温带海域的远洋中层水体，活体很少被人类看见。
zh.stageSummary: 海蛇传说背后, 世界上最长的辐鳍鱼。
zh.summary: “它是世界上最长的辐鳍鱼。它的形状像带子，侧向狭窄，背鳍沿全身延伸，胸鳍短小，腹鳍很长、呈桨状；它的英文俗名也由此而来。它的体色为银色和蓝色，并带有深色斑点，鳍为深红色。” - Wiki

new-insight.title: 海蛇传说的来源
new-insight.body: “它的身体特征和波动式游泳方式，使人推测它可能是许多‘海蛇’目击事件的来源。2016 年，电视节目 River Monsters 得出结论：海蛇神话最可能的来源是皇带鱼。” - Wiki

new-insight-2.title: 行为方式充满未知
new-insight-2.body: “人们对皇带鱼行为所知很少。它曾被观察到通过背鳍波动游泳，也曾被观察到以垂直姿态游动，同时使用身体和背鳍的波动。2010 年，科学家在墨西哥湾中层带拍摄到一条皇带鱼，这是第一段在自然环境中可靠识别皇带鱼的影像。画面显示这条鱼以柱状姿态游动，尾部向下。2016 年，River Monsters 在地中海拍到两条很可能是 R. glesne 的皇带鱼。Jeremy Wade 形容它们在水中优雅而快速；停在锚链旁时，两条鱼似乎都更偏好垂直姿态，尾部向下。” - Wiki

new-insight-3.title: 自截尾部
new-insight-3.body: “皇带鱼显示出泄殖孔后方身体自截的证据。这种自截可能只涉及尾鳍和少数椎骨，也可能包括整个身体后段。由于 R. glesne 的器官集中在身体前部，这些自截不会损伤任何重要器官。记录显示这种自截会在一生中发生数次；所有超过 1.5 米的鱼，身体都会因此变短。为什么会发生这种自截仍不清楚。” - Wiki

new-insight-4.title: 动物保护
new-insight-4.body: “人类对皇带鱼不进行商业捕捞，但偶尔会成为商业渔网的兼捕。煮熟后，皇带鱼的味道被形容为‘像纸’。巨型皇带鱼和近缘的 R. russelii 有时被称为‘地震鱼’，因为大众认为它们会在地震前后浮出水面，不过这种相关性并不受支持。由于体型巨大、身体细长、游泳方式呈波动状，巨型皇带鱼被认为解释了部分海蛇目击。它过去被认为罕见，现在则被怀疑相对常见；只是健康个体在自然栖息地被看见仍然少见。” - Wiki

stageSummary: A living silver ribbon behind sea-serpent legends, made quieter and stranger by real fish anatomy rather than fantasy.
